body.text: China's President Xi Jinping during the trilateral meeting with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, 19 November 2026 (Andres Martinez via Getty Images)
Beijing stockpiled oil and talked neutrality ahead of the Iran war, allowing it to sit above the fighting and the fallout.

For a summit that was billed as a historic opportunity to end the Iran war and promote world peace, last week’s trilateral meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia, and China was a decided letdown. A joint declaration on “the current international situation” released after the meeting in Shenzhen made no mention of the wars in Iran – or Ukraine – and made no concrete commitments to enhancing international security.

For those hoping that China’s President Xi Jinping would help US President Donald Trump find an exit from the Iran war, the summit also demonstrated that Beijing is unlikely to assume the role of official mediator in a high-risk conflict with little chance of success. Indeed, China’s response to the US–Iran war has been both opportunistic and pragmatic, serving its reputational interests across the Global South while insulating itself from the conflict’s worst economic ramifications.

In many ways, China was prepared for the Iran war. By December 2025 – as Trump was threatening military action against Iran – China had built up the world’s largest crude oil reserves, in part by importing sanctioned, cheap oil supplies from Russia and Iran through so-called teapot refineries. As a result of this buildup, Beijing had an estimated 1.4 billion barrels in storage facilities – or around 110–140 days of net imports – reducing its energy reliance on the Strait of Hormuz.
China has publicly committed itself to promoting peace talks even as it has reportedly armed Iran with missile systems and dual-use components that can be used to make drones.

China’s oil reserves, alongside its investments in non-fossil fuels that have boosted the electrification of its economy, enabled it to weather the latest energy crisis fairly well – especially compared to other Asian nations that were forced to either pay more for energy or reduce consumption. For Beijing, this experience validated longstanding strategic concerns over maritime chokepoints – including those along the Malacca–Taiwan corridor – and demonstrated the importance of reducing its dependence on them through a low-carbon industrial policy. It also demonstrated Beijing’s ability to create a “geoeconomic tool” to protect the country’s energy security and influence global oil prices by reducing demand.

The Iran war has offered Beijing insights into the limitations of current US military capabilities and the efficacy of global economic warfare. While the past months have shown that Iran cannot defeat the US, its use of asymmetric tactics across the Gulf has laid bare the weaknesses of costly interceptor systems deployed by the US and its allies to effectively deter against cheap missiles and drones – a tactic that has been used successfully by a range of actors across the Middle East, including the Houthis. Washington’s rapid depletion of precision-guided weapons and air-defence interceptors has also exposed shortfalls in critical stockpiles that would be needed to defend Taiwan from a Chinese invasion and raised questions about US readiness, especially as US military assets have been pulled from the Indo-Pacific to the Middle East.

Washington’s latest regime change war in the Middle East – and its inability to find a good exit strategy – serves Chinese reputational interests, too. While Beijing is not interested in taking on a security role in the Middle East, its official rhetoric and vision for the region – focused on adherence to non-interference, national self-determination, and commitment to (a selective) international law – seeks to provide a clear contrast with the United States. Beijing’s official “neutral narrative” is popular in the Middle East; in recent years, polls have shown that Middle East publics hold more positive views of China than the United States.

Yet, despite the rhetoric, China is not a neutral actor. Even as China has publicly committed itself to “promoting peace talks” and securing a ceasefire in the US–Iran war, it has reportedly armed Iran with missile systems and dual-use components that can be used to make drones. Satellite imagery and intelligence provided by China have enabled Iran to threaten ships in Hormuz and launch precision strikes on US bases in the Middle East. Iranian-backed Houthi militants are reportedly also using Chinese-delivered parts to produce their own ballistic missiles and enhance their military autonomy as they – once again – engage in new fighting with Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, just as in 2024, China has sought to cut a separate deal with the Houthis to enable maritime transits from Saudi Arabia through the Bab el-Mandeb and prevent tanker attacks.

Amid these linkages, Chinese mediation efforts are likely to be limited in nature. While China has increased its regional mediation involvement in recent years, its engagement – as demonstrated in the 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement and the Israel-Palestine conflict – is still characterised by a form of quasi-mediation diplomacy that is high on symbolism while minimising political risk. Though China appears to share the US interest in stemming Iranian nuclear proliferation, Beijing likely sees some strategic advantage in Washington’s attention being diverted from the Asia Pacific. Meanwhile, China’s ability to fully restrain and influence Iranian behaviour – and secure an effective diplomatic off-ramp – remains unclear.

For now, then, China appears to have every reason to speak of peace but limited reason to push for it. As the Shenzhen summit made clear, if Trump wants an exit from Iran, he will have to find it without Xi.

Grace Wermenbol is a senior visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, a senior fellow at the Hague Centre for Strategic Studies, and an adjunct professor at Georgetown University. She is the Executive Director of Boussole Mondiale, a boutique geopolitical analysis firm based in Paris.
